Unsavory is an adjective. It has two layers of meaning — a literal one and a figurative one. In modern English, the figurative meaning is far more common, but knowing both gives you a complete picture.

Unsavory describes food or smells that are unpleasant — something that tastes bad, smells bad, or is unappetizing. If a dish is described as unsavory, your mouth and nose are unhappy.

Example: "The soup had an unsavory smell, so no one touched it."

You won't hear the word used this way very often in modern English. Its real power lies in the figurative meaning.
The Figurative Meaning — Where the Word Truly Lives

In everyday use, unsavory describes something — or someone — that is morally unpleasant, questionable, disreputable, or ethically offensive. Think of it this way: just as unsavory food disgusts your tongue, an unsavory person or situation disgusts your conscience.

When you call a person unsavory, you are saying they have bad morals, a shady reputation, or they are someone that honest, decent people would want to avoid. They may be dishonest, corrupt, or involved in questionable activities.

Example: "She was warned not to trust him — he was known as an unsavory character."
(This means he was shady, untrustworthy, and morally suspect.)

When you call a situation, deal, or practice unsavory, you are saying it feels ethically wrong, dirty, or morally uncomfortable — even if it might not be outright illegal.

Example: "The politician was linked to several unsavory business arrangements."
(This means the dealings felt corrupt, dishonest, or beneath acceptable moral standards.)

Unsavory is a word of moral judgment. It doesn't just say something is "bad." It says something is bad in a way that causes disgust, unease, and a desire to distance yourself from it. It implies that a respectable, honest person would find it offensive or deeply uncomfortable.

Importantly, unsavory sits at a specific point on the scale of negativity. It is not the harshest word — something unsavory isn't necessarily criminal or outright evil. It occupies the space between "slightly off" and "clearly wrong." It's the word you use when something doesn't quite cross the clearest lines, but it still makes your skin crawl or makes you feel uneasy. It's morally grimy.

This is important. Unsavory does not simply mean "annoying," "unfriendly," "boring," or "rude." It specifically carries a sense of moral or ethical distaste. A loud neighbor is not unsavory. A con artist who tricks elderly people out of their savings — that is unsavory.
What Is Commonly Described as Unsavory

In practice, you will often see these combinations:

An unsavory character / figure / individual — a person of questionable morals or a shady reputation. An unsavory reputation — a name known for dishonesty or disreputable behavior. An unsavory deal / practice / arrangement — a business or transaction that feels ethically dirty. An unsavory topic — a subject that is morally uncomfortable to bring up. An unsavory history — a past filled with shameful or questionable events.
A Simple Way to Lock the Meaning in Your Memory

Think of the word "savor." When you savor something, you enjoy it deeply — it's wonderful, pleasing, and something you want more of. Now place "un-" in front of it. Unsavory is the complete opposite: something you don't want anywhere near you, something that makes you feel morally disgusted or deeply uncomfortable. The prefix "un-" simply flips the meaning to its negative.

The word is slightly formal and somewhat literary in tone. Native speakers tend to use it in writing, in news articles, or in careful speech. You would not typically hear it in very casual conversation (where someone might just say "shady" or "sketchy" instead). Knowing this helps you understand when and where to use it — and when to expect it.
